summary: US-023: A selection that would strand a lone seat is refused, per the map's own rule
description:
**As** an organizer, **I want** the system to stop buyers leaving single unsellable seats between parties, **so that** I do not finish the on-sale with a row full of gaps I can never sell.

**Priority:** P2  **Depends on:** TKT-174 (a picker to refuse a selection in)

**The third epic COS**, and the only one with no existing machinery: *"Orphan-single-seat prevention rules configurable per map."* An orphan is a free seat with no free neighbour left in its row after a selection is taken. Preventing it is standard practice in reserved seating and is worth real revenue; making it **configurable per map** matters because the rule is wrong for some venues (general-admission-style rows, boxes, accessible pairs).

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- [ ] A seat map carries an orphan-prevention setting owned by catalog alongside the geometry, defaulting to **off** so every existing map behaves exactly as it does today.
- [ ] With the rule on, a seat selection whose commitment would leave a free seat with no free neighbour in its row is refused **server-side, at claim time** — the arbiter is the same transaction that decides the claim, not the browser. A refusal names the seat(s) that would be stranded.
- [ ] The rule reads the seat map version the pool is seated against, so an edit that republishes the map cannot silently change the rule applied to a live claim (ADR-029: a published version is immutable).
- [ ] With the rule off, behaviour is byte-identical to TKT-173's: no extra read, no extra latency on the claim path.
- [ ] Row ends are handled explicitly and deliberately: a seat at the end of a row has one neighbour, not two, and the rule must state and test what it does there.
- [ ] The picker surfaces the refusal legibly and the map stays usable afterwards (the buyer can adjust the selection without reloading).
- [ ] The rule is exercised under the seated contention test: concurrent claimants cannot each pass the check and jointly strand a seat — the check is only real if it holds under the transaction that decides.
- [ ] Spec declared, generated code committed before the gate, smoke coverage (ADR-009 / ADR-028 / ADR-030).

Quality gates: `make check` green; contract tests; browser submit evidence for the UI surface. **This ticket moves no money.**

objective.note: It is the epic's third COS and the only one with no existing machinery; without it the epic closes incomplete.

scope.note: IN: the per-map setting, server-side enforcement at claim time, row-end semantics, the UI surface, the contention proof. OUT: adjacency-aware best-available (TKT-81), price-tier or accessibility-seat rules, multi-row party splitting, retro-fitting the rule to already-sold maps.

uncertainties.note: Resolved at Planning under the owner-waived gate protocol (was owner: human). **Where the check runs is a real architectural decision, not a coin flip.** Inventory decides the claim and knows occupancy but holds seat identities as opaque `section/row/seat` strings — it has no row ordering. Catalog owns the geometry and the rule but does not decide claims. Three candidate shapes: (a) inventory calls catalog on the claim path — simplest, but puts a synchronous cross-service call inside the hottest transaction in the system, which ADR-010 exists to keep short; (b) inventory caches the row layout from the `seat_map.published` event it already consumes — no hot-path call, at the cost of a projection to keep correct; (c) the check runs in commerce between the price resolution and the claim — no hot-path cost, but it is then advisory, and a check that does not run inside the deciding transaction cannot satisfy the contention AC. Planning must choose and record a reason; the choice likely warrants an ADR.

dependencies.note: blocked-by TKT-174. Nothing outside this epic is open.

approach.note: Follows from the uncertainty above. Inventory's consumer already receives catalog seat-map events and already holds a catalog HTTP client for pinning, so both (a) and (b) have an existing seam — which one is right is Planning's call.

first_slice.note: A single row of five seats with the rule on: selecting seats 1 and 2 is refused because seat 3 would strand against an already-taken 4; selecting 1-3 succeeds.

success.note: Demoable in the browser: turn the rule on for a map, try to strand a seat, get refused with the seat named.

context_memo.note: Baked at decomposition (2026-08-01). Re-resolve at claim — this is the last ticket of the epic and three others land before it.

binding.rule: Local gate: `make check` (lint + test + build, Go & TS, plus the gateway smoke suite; run `make deps` first on a clean clone). CI runs the same gate — keep them mirrored. Commit regenerated code (`openapi_gen.go`, `api-types.gen.ts`) before running the gate — `check-generate` diffs against HEAD, so an uncommitted regen reads as drift and fails the run.

reference.summary: Epic lineage and capability map (US-017/US-018 are the seat-claim core; this epic is the buyer-facing picker)

governingAdrs.why: The claim transaction is the hottest path in the platform and is deliberately kept short and lock-ordered. A synchronous cross-service call added inside it is the single most expensive thing this ticket could do — if Planning chooses that shape, it must justify it against this ADR, not around it.

Seat claim/pin coordination: `released_at IS NULL` is liveness, and expired holds are swept lazily. An orphan check that counts a lazily-unswept expired hold as occupying a seat will refuse a legal selection.

A published seat-map version is immutable and an edit mints a NEW version; a pool is seated against one specific version. The rule and the geometry it reads must both come from the version the pool names, or a republish silently changes the rule under a live claim. Also: the family-scoped advisory lock, not a row lock, is what closes the edit-vs-claim race.

If the check reads geometry, it reads the hours tier — legitimately cacheable. If it reads occupancy, that is the seconds tier and inside the deciding transaction it must not be read from any cache at all.
Whatever query backs the rule, a scoped read is only scoped if an index backs the filter — and proving it takes two tests.
Contract-first: the per-map setting is a catalog contract change; generated code committed before the gate.

comments.body:
<!-- sdlc:stage=ready kind=claim -->
### Claimed — TKT-175

**Selection reason.** The epic's last child. Its only blocker, TKT-174, merged as `762ee6fc`. Nothing else in flight.

**Blocker check.** `blocked-by TKT-174` — Done. Zero open blockers.

**Branch.** `TKT-175-orphan-seat-rules`, cut from `origin/main` at `762ee6fc`.

**⚠️ Gate waiver.** Runs **gateless** under the standing owner waiver for TKT-35. Recorded again here: this is the fourth and last child to run without human gates, and the epic therefore closes with **no control arm** — TKT-173's and TKT-174's retros both asked for one and both were overruled by the standing instruction, correctly.

**Model routing** unchanged: plan `gpt-5.6-sol` · planReview `main-agent` · implement `main-agent` · aiReview `gpt-5.6-sol`. Both cross-model pairs differ. ✅

---

### This ticket carries the epic's only genuine architectural decision

The other three children had implementation choices. This one has a boundary problem, and it was recorded at decomposition rather than discovered late:

> Inventory decides the claim and knows occupancy, but holds seat identities as **opaque `section/row/seat` strings** — it has no row ordering. Catalog owns the geometry and the rule but does not decide claims.

An orphan is a free seat with no free neighbour left **in its row** after a selection is taken. Deciding that needs the row's ordered seats *and* live occupancy *and* the deciding transaction — and no single service has all three today.

**One fact checked at claim time that narrows the field:** inventory does **not** consume seat-map events. `services/inventory/internal/consumer/consumer.go` filters exactly four subjects — `performance.published`, `.archived`, `.closed`, `.reopened`. There is no `seat_map.published` subscription and no geometry projection. So the "inventory keeps a cached row layout" option is not a small addition to an existing consumer; it is a new subscription, a new projection, and a new thing that can be stale. The decomposition note called it "no hot-path call, at the cost of a projection to keep correct" — the cost is larger than that phrasing suggests, and Planning should price it honestly.

### Stop-condition pre-check

- **Auth:** untouched.
- **Money:** untouched — this refuses a claim, it prices nothing.
- **Data migrations:** at least one is likely (a per-map setting in catalog). Additive settings on an existing table are anticipated by the ticket's own AC ("a seat map carries an orphan-prevention setting owned by catalog"). Anything beyond that — a new table for a geometry projection in inventory, say — is a consequence of the architectural choice and must be **named in the plan before it is written**, not discovered in the diff.
- **CI/deploy:** none expected.
- **The hot path:** ADR-010's claim transaction is the platform's most contended. If the plan puts a synchronous cross-service call inside it, that is a decision requiring an explicit argument against ADR-010, and it is the one thing on this ticket I will not accept by default.

### Scope reminder

IN: the per-map setting, server-side enforcement at claim time, row-end semantics, the picker's surfacing of the refusal, the contention proof. OUT: adjacency-aware best-available (TKT-81), price-tier or accessibility-seat rules, multi-row party splitting, retro-fitting the rule to already-sold maps.
